subject: mathematics
question_text: If Cos⁻¹(p/a) + Cos⁻¹(q/b) = α, prove that p²/a² − (2pq/(ab)) cosα + q²/b² = sin²α.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.114, chapter 10 INVERSE TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS, Short Answer question 7. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split is 1+1+1+1 because the four moves are genuinely separate — naming the angles with their domain, expanding the sum, squaring, and rearranging to sin²α. NOTATION: the book prints the inverse functions in lower case (cos⁻¹); they are written here with capitals to match the principal-value convention used across the rest of this unit. The identity was checked numerically to twelve decimal places on four independent quadruples (p,a,q,b) = (3,5,5,13), (1,2,2,3), (−1,4,3,7) and (0.3,1,−0.8,1); left and right sides agreed in every case. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, at 4 marks each, under the 2026-27 pattern; Inverse Trigonometric Functions is an SAQ-only unit, so the paper gives it no Section-A and no Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. LINES EXPANDED 2026-09-14 (founder direction, modelled on the Maths-2A and Maths-2B expansions): every move is written on its own line, with the reason or the arithmetic shown before it is used; the steps, marks and split are unchanged.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each move in order, and say which formula you reach for and why.
formula_note: Cos⁻¹(p/a) and Cos⁻¹(q/b) both lie in [0, π], where sine is never negative — so sinA = √(1−p²/a²) and sinB = √(1−q²/b²) take the positive root for any value of p/a or q/b, not only when it is positive. This differs from Sin⁻¹ or Tan⁻¹ pairs, where it is the cosine that is instead guaranteed non-negative.

steps.label: Name the two angles
steps.margin_note: First mark. The domain lines are part of the answer: without |p/a| ≤ 1 and |q/b| ≤ 1 the two inverse cosines do not exist.
steps.memory_tip: Cos⁻¹ gives an angle in [0, π], and sine is never negative there. The proof then works with sin²A and sin²B only.
lines: (Cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π], where sine is never negative)

recall.must_convey: That A and B are named, the domain conditions are written, and both sines are non-negative.
accept: let a be cos inverse p over a and b be cos inverse q over b, with both fractions between minus one and one

write the domain first, p by a and q by b must be at most one in size
domain rasali, p by a and q by b modulus one kanna thakkuva
the sum of the two angles is alpha

steps.why: Cos⁻¹ returns an angle in [0, π], where sine is never negative. The proof squares sinA sinB, so it uses only sin²A = 1 − cos²A and needs no sign choice.
common_mistakes: Writing A or B outside [0, π].

steps.label: Expand cos of the sum
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Keep the product of the sines alone on one side — the next step squares that line.
steps.memory_tip: Move the sine product to one side by itself. Everything else is already known in p, q, a and b.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A + B) is expanded and the product sinA sinB is isolated as pq/(ab) − cosα.
accept: expand cos of a plus b as cos cos minus sin sin and make the sine product the subject
sin a sin b equals p q over a b minus cos alpha
isolate the product of the sines before squaring
sin product ni okka side ki teeskoni ravali
the sine product is p q by a b minus cos alpha

steps.why: Isolating the product of the sines means one squaring step turns it into sin²A sin²B, which can be written with cosA = p/a and cosB = q/b.
common_mistakes: Writing cos(A + B) with a plus between the two products.
Leaving the sine product mixed with the other terms.

steps.label: Square both sides
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Squaring both sides of a true equation always gives a true equation, so nothing extra has to be checked here.
steps.memory_tip: Square once. The term p²q²/(a²b²) appears on both sides and cancels.

lines.text: (square both sides of the last line)

recall.must_convey: That both sides are squared, the sines are replaced by 1 − p²/a² and 1 − q²/b², and p²q²/(a²b²) cancels.
accept: square both sides and replace sin squared a by one minus p squared over a squared
the p squared q squared term appears on both sides and cancels
expand the square of the difference with its middle term
square chesthe p squared q squared term rendu vaipula cancel avthundi
squaring removes both square roots at once

steps.why: Squaring turns sinA sinB into sin²A sin²B, which can be written with cosA = p/a and cosB = q/b. The term p²q²/(a²b²) then appears on both sides and cancels, which is what leaves a clean identity.
common_mistakes: Squaring only one side of the equation.
Expanding the square of a difference without its middle term.

steps.label: Rearrange to the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Write the three terms in the order the question asks so an examiner can match them line for line.
steps.memory_tip: Finish with 1 − cos²α = sin²α — the whole right-hand side of the question is only that.

recall.must_convey: That the terms are rearranged and 1 − cos²α is replaced by sin²α.

steps.why: The last move is only the Pythagorean identity: 1 − cos²α is sin²α. Everything before it was rearrangement.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 1 − cos²α without writing sin²α.
Losing the sign of the middle term.
